st.t: Task allocation: AI redistributes skill and responsibility

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s labour-market claim with large-scale US payroll evidence showing concentrated employment weakness among young workers in highly AI-exposed occupations, particularly where usage is classified as automation. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution: the findings are not legal-sector-specific, causation remains unresolved, and they do not demonstrate profession-wide displacement.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s cautious labour-market framing and materially extends it with economy-wide payroll evidence that employment declines are concentrated among young workers in highly AI-exposed, automation-heavy occupations, while augmentation-heavy occupations fare better. It also preserves the cluster’s uncertainty by treating the association as consistent with, rather than definitive proof of, an AI effect; its findings are not legal-sector-specific.
qs: In contrast, for the highest two  exposure quintiles employment for 22-25 year olds declined by 6% between late 2022 and September  2025, while employment for workers aged 35-49 grew by over 8%.

While our main estimates may be influenced by factors other than generative AI, our results  are consistent with the hypothesis that generative AI has begun to affect entry-level employment  significantly.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal distinction between productivity and career outcomes: it reports concentrated early-career employment declines in highly AI-exposed occupations and explicitly notes that productivity gains can either increase or reduce employment. It appropriately treats AI causation and longer-term effects as unresolved.
qs: • After conditioning on firm-time effects, young workers experienced a 16% relative employment        decline in the most exposed occupations.

2      Improved productivity of workers in an occupation could lead to either reduced or increased employment, de- pending on, among other things, how elastic demand is for the output of those workers.

st.t: Early careers: Comparative design yields no findings
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis: it documents age- and exposure-based employment comparisons, inflation-adjusted compensation measures and alternative sample definitions, while the supplied excerpts do not preserve trends or estimates sufficient to establish AI displacement, causal effects or legal-sector staffing consequences.
qs: Annual base compensation is deflated to 2017 dollars using the PCE deflator.

st.t: Entry routes: Reduced hiring precedes broader displacement
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition by documenting concentrated employment declines among workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations despite growth among older workers, and by identifying reduced junior hiring as a plausible adjustment mechanism. Its support is qualified: the hiring mechanism remains to be tested, and the authors do not claim that generative AI is the sole cause or forecast economy-wide displacement.
qs: In contrast, workers  aged 22 to 25 have experienced a 6% decline in employment from late 2022 to September 2025 in  the most AI-exposed occupations, compared to a 6-9% increase for older workers.

While our main estimates may be influenced by factors other than generative AI, our results  are consistent with the hypothesis that generative AI has begun to affect entry-level employment  significantly.

st.t: Graduate employment: Weakness signals but does not prove displacement
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious conclusion: it treats graduate-hiring declines as consistent with early-career weakness while emphasizing volatile subgroup estimates and conflicting job-posting evidence. It therefore supplies signals of possible displacement but not a stable causal estimate attributable to AI.
qs: SignalFire finds steep declines in new graduate hires in the tech sector compared to pre-Pandemic levels (Doshay and Bantock, 2025), consistent with the findings in this paper.

Though there are  millions of workers employed in these professions across the US, the estimates are highly volatile,  with common fluctuations of 20% or greater in estimated employment month-to-month.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that labour-market adjustment may occur through reduced junior hiring rather than incumbent displacement, while experienced workers benefit from complementary AI use. It appropriately presents this mechanism as a prediction requiring further modelling and testing, not as an established causal effect.
qs: Consequently firms may primarily  shrink junior inflows rather than displace incumbents.
An important direction for  research is to further model and test these predictions.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s caution against inferring uniform productivity or worker replacement from AI capability gains. It frames technological effects as heterogeneous and possible early labor-market signals rather than established displacement, but provides no direct evidence on durable skill formation in this excerpt.
qs: Historically, technologies have affected different  tasks, occupations, and industries in different ways, replacing work in some, augmenting others,  and transforming still others.
These heterogeneous effects suggest that there may be “canaries in  the coal mine” which are harbingers of more widespread effects of AI.

st.t: Labour evidence: Distinct mechanisms resist one AI effect
st.an: The source summary supports the cluster’s methodological conclusion that this excerpt cannot establish substantive labour-market effects or legal-staffing implications. Its lack of interpretable claims is consistent with separating usable evidence from fragments that cannot support inference.

st.t: Young workers: Automation differs from augmentation effects
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core finding that employment weakness is concentrated among highly AI-exposed workers aged 22–25, with smaller, insignificant estimates for older groups. It also distinguishes automation from augmentation and reports that related results persist after excluding low-usage occupations, although the supplied excerpts do not independently show the direction or magnitude of the automation–augmentation difference.
qs: For workers aged  22-25, estimates for higher quintiles are large and statistically significant, with a 15 log point de-  cline in relative employment comparable in magnitude to the estimates in the raw data in Figure 2.
Figures A9 and A10 show that automation and augmentation results are similar when dropping occupations with low overall Claude usage.

st.t: Youth employment: Exposure measures require competing tests
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s methodological conclusion: it compares age groups using an occupational AI-exposure proxy, tests alternative samples and data sources, and examines compensation as well as employment. The supplied excerpts document research design rather than readable effects or causal evidence of entry-level displacement.
qs: Exposure quintiles are defined based on the GPT-4 β measures from Eloundou et al.

kp.k: Large-scale payroll data track employment through September 2025
kp.d: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen examine US employment across occupations, rather than legal services specifically. Their main ADP sample contains 3.5–5 million workers monthly, retaining firms with earnings records every month from January 2021 through September 2025. They include workers under 70 with positive earnings and recorded job titles, excluding part-time employees. Job titles are mapped to occupational codes and linked to AI exposure measures. ADP's firm distribution does not exactly match the broader economy, and its clients tend to grow faster on average.
qs: We include only workers with positive earnings, exclude part-time employees, and subset to people under age 70.
ADP observes job titles for about 70% of workers in its system.
We maintain a consistent set of firms by keeping only companies that have employee earnings records for each month from January 2021 through September 2025.

kp.k: Young workers experience disproportionate declines in exposed occupations
kp.d: The November 2025 revision reports a 16% relative employment decline for workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations after conditioning on firm-time effects. The results section separately describes the regression estimate as a 15 log-point decline; these are the paper's distinct reported formulations. Employment for older workers generally remains stable or grows. Among software developers aged 22–25, employment fell nearly 20% from its late-2022 peak by September 2025, whereas less-exposed occupations such as health aides exhibit different age patterns.
qs: By September 2025, employment for software developers aged 22-25 declined nearly 20% compared to its peak
employment for young workers has been growing faster than for older workers.
a 15 log point decline in relative employment

kp.k: Exposed jobs drive stagnant employment growth among young workers
kp.d: Between late 2022 and September 2025, employment across the lowest three AI-exposure quintiles grew 5–13% for each age group, without a clear age ordering. Across the highest two exposure quintiles, employment for 22–25-year-olds declined 6%, while employment for workers aged 35–49 increased over 8%. The authors interpret this divergence as driving weak overall employment growth among young workers despite continued aggregate growth in ADP employment; they caution that these descriptive comparisons could reflect other economic changes.
qs: employment growth from late 2022 to September 2025 was 5-13% for the lowest three AI exposure quintiles
while employment for workers aged 35-49 grew by over 8%.
we caution the trends observed in these first two facts could be driven by other changes in the US

kp.k: Automation and augmentation show different employment associations
kp.d: The study combines Eloundou et al.'s GPT-4 β occupational exposure measure with Anthropic Economic Index data from several million Claude conversations. The latter classifies task-related conversations as automative, augmentative or neither, providing proxies for substitution versus complementarity rather than direct measurements of sampled firms' adoption. Young-worker employment declines are concentrated in occupations with high estimated automation shares. Employment is not similarly ordered by augmentation exposure: the highest augmentation quintile has among the fastest growth. Results remain similar after excluding occupations with low overall Claude usage.
qs: We focus on the GPT-4 based β exposure measures from their paper.
the occupations with the highest estimated automation shares have experienced declining employment for the youngest workers.
Employment changes for young workers are not ordered by augmentation exposure, as the fifth quintile has among the fastest employment growth.

kp.k: Within-firm controls preserve the young-worker employment pattern
kp.d: Separate Poisson event-study regressions by age group control for firm-time and firm-exposure-quintile fixed effects, with October 2022 as the reference month and standard errors clustered by firm. Higher-exposure estimates for ages 22–25 are large and statistically significant; estimates for other ages are generally smaller and not statistically significant. Firm-time effects absorb shocks affecting exposure groups equally within a firm, but cannot eliminate occupation-specific confounding within firms, such as differential post-pandemic overhiring.
qs: The firm-time effects absorb aggregate firm shocks that impact each exposure quintile equally.
The firm-quintile effects adjust for baseline differences in hiring across quintiles within the firm.
Standard errors are clustered by firm.

Estimates for other age groups are generally much smaller in magnitude and not statistically sig-

kp.k: Adjustment appears more in employment than base compensation
kp.d: Annual base compensation shows little divergence by age or AI exposure, unlike employment. Compensation is deflated to 2017 dollars and observed through August 2025, rather than the September employment endpoint. The measure excludes additional components such as bonuses, equity, commissions and overtime. Wage stickiness and offsetting effects of replacing expert versus inexpert tasks are offered as possible explanations, not established mechanisms.
qs: We find little difference in compensation trends by age or exposure quintile.
results for compensation end in August 2025
The limited changes we find for wages suggest that these effects may be offsetting, at least in the short run.

kp.k: Robustness checks weaken several competing explanations
kp.d: Patterns broadly survive excluding computer occupations and technology firms, separating teleworkable from non-teleworkable occupations, stratifying occupational interest-rate exposure, analysing men and women separately, allowing firm entry and exit, and including part-time and temporary workers. The longer sample introduces an important qualification: the highest Eloundou exposure quintile had slower growth beginning around 2020, whereas Anthropic-based measures show comparable pre-generative-AI growth followed by divergence. The authors therefore do not present uniformly clean pre-trends across every measure.
qs: These results indicate that our findings are not specific to technology roles.
A concern is that for the Eloundou et al. (2024) measures the most exposed quintile had slower employment growth starting around 2020.
For these measures the most exposed groups have comparable employment growth throughout the period before generative AI, with divergent trends afterwards.

kp.k: Experience may protect non-college workers less
kp.d: Analyses distinguish occupations with more than 70% college graduates from those with fewer than 30%, using 2017 ACS occupational education shares rather than individual educational attainment. High-college-share occupations exhibit declining employment overall and more muted exposure differences. Low-college-share occupations grow overall but show declining employment in the most exposed jobs, with exposure-related divergence extending to workers up to age 40. The authors conclude that pandemic-related educational deterioration cannot fully explain their main findings.
qs: These findings suggest that deteriorating education outcomes cannot fully explain our main results.
They also suggest that for non-college workers, experience may serve as less of a buffer to labor market disruption than for college workers.

kp.k: Codified knowledge substitution offers a proposed mechanism
kp.d: The authors hypothesise that AI substitutes more readily for codified knowledge supplied by new workers than for tacit knowledge accumulated through experience. They suggest that this could eliminate checkable entry-level tasks while complementing experienced workers' judgment, client and process work. Additional proposed mechanisms include increased experienced-worker span of control, reduced hiring as a low-friction adjustment, and weak incentives to train juniors who may leave. These mechanisms require further modelling and testing; the paper does not establish that reduced hiring rather than layoffs accounts for the measured declines.
qs: AI may be less capable of replacing tacit knowledge
Consequently firms may primarily shrink junior inflows rather than displace incumbents.
An important direction for research is to further model and test these predictions.

kp.k: Findings remain suggestive rather than definitive causal evidence
kp.d: The authors describe their results as consistent with generative AI beginning to affect entry-level employment, while explicitly allowing other contributing factors. They recommend continued monitoring and better firm-level AI adoption data to sharpen causal estimation. They also report mixed external evidence, including similar entry-level declines in US and UK LinkedIn studies but minimal entry-level earnings or hours effects in Denmark. Predictions of large future job losses, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's forecast of roughly 50% of entry-level white-collar jobs within five years, are reported context rather than this paper's empirical finding or forecast.
qs: While we explore a variety of alternative explanations, we caution that the facts we document
may in part be influenced by factors other than generative AI.

kp.k: Small survey cells complicate independent comparisons
kp.d: The paper's CPS comparisons show highly volatile age-occupation employment estimates, including common monthly fluctuations of 20% or greater. Monthly CPS cells contain only 26–53 software developers aged 22–25, 49–95 young customer service representatives and 2–14 young home health aides. The authors attribute this volatility to small samples and a sampling design not targeted at these subgroups, and encourage validation with larger sources such as the ACS, while recognising its publication lag.
qs: The CPS includes between 26 and 53 young software developers aged between 22 and 25 per month over our sample period.
It includes between 49 and 95 young customer service representatives, and between 2 and 14 young home health aides.
We encourage comparison of our findings to results from other data sources

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen report employment patterns consistent with generative AI disproportionately reducing entry-level employment in exposed US occupations, rather than an economy-wide employment contraction.
pts.d: In the November 13, 2025 revision, the authors report a 16% relative employment decline for workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations after conditioning on firm-time effects. The results section separately describes the regression magnitude as 15 log points; these are retained as the source's reported descriptions rather than treated as identical numerical measures. The unadjusted employment decline in the highest two exposure quintiles was 6% between late 2022 and September 2025, while employment for workers aged 35–49 grew by over 8%. Young software developers experienced a nearly 20% decline from their late-2022 peak. These are cross-domain labour-market claims, not findings specifically about lawyers or legal services.

pts.k: The authors associate entry-level employment declines with automative AI uses, not with the most augmentative uses.
pts.d: Occupations with the highest estimated automation shares show declining employment among workers aged 22–25. Employment is not similarly ordered by augmentation exposure: the highest augmentation quintile is among those with the fastest employment growth. The authors interpret this as consistent with substitution in automative applications and complementarity in augmentative applications, rather than demonstrating the causal effect of a particular employer's AI deployment.

pts.k: Employment, rather than base compensation, is the main observed adjustment margin.
pts.d: The authors find little divergence in annual base salary trends across age groups or AI-exposure quintiles. They offer short-run wage stickiness or offsetting wage effects from displacement of expert and inexpert tasks as possible explanations, not established mechanisms. Base compensation excludes potentially important components such as bonuses, commissions and equity.

pts.k: The authors propose that AI substitutes for codified junior tasks while complementing experience, and that firms may adjust through reduced junior hiring.
pts.d: These are explanatory hypotheses requiring further testing. The authors suggest that younger workers supply relatively more codified knowledge, whereas experienced workers possess tacit knowledge and perform judgment-, client- and process-intensive tasks that may be harder to replace. AI may also expand experienced staff's effective span of control. Reduced recruitment may be easier than displacing incumbents, particularly when employers have weak incentives to train juniors who may leave. The source's discussion of experienced staff's leverage concerns span of control, not a measured law-firm associate-to-partner ratio.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The empirical basis is a large ADP payroll panel linked to occupational AI-exposure and Claude-use measures.
pts.d: The main sample contains approximately 3.5–5 million workers each month at firms continuously observed from January 2021 through September 2025. It includes positive-earnings workers under 70 with recorded job titles and excludes part-time employees. ADP job titles are mapped to occupational codes and linked to Eloundou et al.'s GPT-4 β exposure measures and Handa et al.'s Anthropic Economic Index. Claude conversations provide occupational proxies for automation and augmentation, not direct measures of adoption at the sampled employers. Age-specific Poisson event studies control for firm-time and firm-quintile effects, with standard errors clustered by firm. The authors test alternative samples excluding computer occupations and technology firms, separating teleworkability and interest-rate exposure, extending the historical period, and varying education composition, gender and sample restrictions. CPS comparisons are too noisy in fine age-occupation groups to provide a precise independent check.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern the period following late-2022 generative-AI proliferation through September 2025; causality and longer-term outcomes remain qualified.
pts.d: The main employment comparisons use October 2022 as the reference month. Compensation results end in August 2025 because of deflator availability. The authors explicitly allow for non-AI explanations and call for better firm-level adoption data to estimate causal effects. Firm-time controls absorb common firm shocks, not every within-firm occupation-specific shock. Longer historical checks generally support post-2022 divergence, although the GPT-4-based highest-exposure group already had slower growth around 2020; the authors say this pre-pattern does not appear with the Anthropic measures. ADP employers are not fully representative of the US economy. The authors do not make a numerical forecast of future job losses or adopt the quoted external prediction that half of entry-level white-collar jobs could disappear within five years.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The strongest adverse employment pattern affects workers aged 22–25 in highly exposed occupations; experience is a less consistent buffer in occupations with low college shares.
pts.d: Software developers and customer-service representatives are prominent affected examples; marketing and sales managers show a smaller analogous pattern. Older workers in the same exposed occupations generally have more favourable employment trends, while young workers in less-exposed occupations often continue to gain employment. Health aides provide a contrasting example in which younger workers' employment grows faster than older workers'. In occupations with low college shares, employment divergence by AI exposure extends to workers up to age 40. Education is measured through occupational college shares, not each worker's own qualification. Results span technology and nontechnology settings and both men and women. The paper does not separately estimate effects on law firms, ALSPs, legal departments or legal clients.
